difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE because it links two concepts (translating an "except" sentence into a biconditional, and recognising that s1/s2 and s3/s4 are contrapositive pairs), after which a four-row truth table settles all four options in about two to three minutes.
stem:
Let $\mathit{game}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{rugby})$ be true if the ball is used in rugby and false otherwise.

Let $\mathit{shape}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{round})$ be true if the ball is round and false otherwise.

Consider the following logical sentences:

$s1\colon\ \forall \mathit{ball}\ \neg\, \mathit{game}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{rugby}) \Longrightarrow \mathit{shape}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{round})$

$s2\colon\ \forall \mathit{ball}\ \neg\, \mathit{shape}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{round}) \Longrightarrow \mathit{game}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{rugby})$

$s3\colon\ \forall \mathit{ball}\ \mathit{game}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{rugby}) \Longrightarrow \neg\, \mathit{shape}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{round})$

$s4\colon\ \forall \mathit{ball}\ \mathit{shape}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{round}) \Longrightarrow \neg\, \mathit{game}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{rugby})$

Which of the following choices is/are logical representations of the assertion,

“All balls are round except balls used in rugby”?

solution.quick:
Write $G$ for $\mathit{game}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{rugby})$ and $R$ for $\mathit{shape}(\mathit{ball}, \mathit{round})$. Each pair of sentences is a contrapositive pair: $s1 \equiv s2 \equiv  orall \mathit{ball}\,(G \lor R)$ ("every non-rugby ball is round") and $s3 \equiv s4 \equiv  orall \mathit{ball}\,(
eg G \lor 
eg R)$ ("no rugby ball is round"). The assertion needs **both** halves, $R \Leftrightarrow 
eg G$ for every ball, so it takes one sentence from each pair: $s1 \land s3$ and $s2 \land s3$ work, while $s1 \land s2$ and $s3 \land s4$ each state only one half. The answer is **(A), (C)**.

steps.title: Name the atoms and rewrite each sentence as a disjunction
steps.body:
For a ball $b$, let $G$ stand for $\mathit{game}(b, \mathit{rugby})$ ("$b$ is used in rugby") and $R$ for $\mathit{shape}(b, \mathit{round})$ ("$b$ is round"). In each sentence the quantifier $\forall \mathit{ball}$ governs the whole implication, so each sentence says that the implication holds for **every** ball.

Use $p \Rightarrow q \equiv \neg p \lor q$ on each body:

| Sentence | Implication | Equivalent disjunction | In words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $s1$ | $\neg G \Rightarrow R$ | $G \lor R$ | every ball not used in rugby is round |
| $s2$ | $\neg R \Rightarrow G$ | $R \lor G$ | every ball that is not round is a rugby ball |
| $s3$ | $G \Rightarrow \neg R$ | $\neg G \lor \neg R$ | no rugby ball is round |
| $s4$ | $R \Rightarrow \neg G$ | $\neg R \lor \neg G$ | no round ball is a rugby ball |

So $s1 \equiv s2$ and $s3 \equiv s4$: in each pair one sentence is the **contrapositive** of the other ($\neg G \Rightarrow R$ flips to $\neg R \Rightarrow G$). There are really only two different statements here.

steps.title: Translate the assertion
steps.body:
"All balls are round except balls used in rugby" makes two claims:

1. **The rule:** every ball that is not used in rugby is round: $\forall b\ (\neg G \Rightarrow R)$, which is $s1$.
2. **The exception:** the balls used in rugby are exactly the ones excluded from being round, so they are not round: $\forall b\ (G \Rightarrow \neg R)$, which is $s3$.

Together, for every ball, $R \Leftrightarrow \neg G$: a ball is round **if and only if** it is not used in rugby. Equivalently, exactly one of $G$ and $R$ is true for each ball.

Because $\forall$ distributes over $\land$, i.e. $(\forall b\ P) \land (\forall b\ Q) \equiv \forall b\ (P \land Q)$, a conjunction of two of the given sentences is the same as one $\forall$ over the conjunction of their bodies. So each option can be checked ball by ball with a four-row truth table.

steps.title: Truth table for one ball
steps.body:
| $G$ (rugby) | $R$ (round) | $s1$, $s2$: $G \lor R$ | $s3$, $s4$: $\neg G \lor \neg R$ | Assertion: $R \Leftrightarrow \neg G$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| F | F | F | T | F |
| F | T | T | T | T |
| T | F | T | T | T |
| T | T | T | F | F |

- $G \lor R$ rules out only the row F, F (a non-rugby ball that is not round).
- $\neg G \lor \neg R$ rules out only the row T, T (a rugby ball that is round).
- The assertion rules out **both** of those rows.

So the assertion equals $(G \lor R) \land (\neg G \lor \neg R)$: one sentence from $\{s1, s2\}$ **and** one from $\{s3, s4\}$.

steps.title: Check each option
steps.body:
| Option | Reduces to | Rows it rules out | Matches the assertion? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (A) $s1 \land s3$ | $(G \lor R) \land (\neg G \lor \neg R)$ | F,F and T,T | **Yes** |
| (B) $s1 \land s2$ | $G \lor R$ (same sentence twice) | F,F only | No: allows a round rugby ball |
| (C) $s2 \land s3$ | $(G \lor R) \land (\neg G \lor \neg R)$ | F,F and T,T | **Yes** |
| (D) $s3 \land s4$ | $\neg G \lor \neg R$ (same sentence twice) | T,T only | No: allows a non-round ball that is not used in rugby |

(A) and (C) are the same formula, since $s2 \equiv s1$. (B) and (D) each pair a sentence with its own contrapositive, so each states only one half of the assertion. (The combinations $s1 \land s4$ and $s2 \land s4$ would also be correct, but they are not offered.)

The answer is **(A), (C)**.

solution.teaching:
**Translating English into first-order logic.** A sentence such as "All $P$ are $Q$" becomes $\forall x\ (P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x))$: the quantifier says "for every object", and the implication restricts the claim to the objects that have property $P$. With one predicate for "used in rugby" ($G$) and one for "round" ($R$), every English claim in this question is a statement about which of the four combinations of $G$ and $R$ a ball may have.

**Implication and its contrapositive.** $p \Rightarrow q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false, so it is equivalent to $\neg p \lor q$. Swapping and negating both sides gives the **contrapositive** $\neg q \Rightarrow \neg p$, which is also $\neg p \lor q$: an implication and its contrapositive always say the same thing. Do not confuse it with the **converse** $q \Rightarrow p$, which says something different. Here $s2$ is the contrapositive of $s1$, and $s4$ is the contrapositive of $s3$, so four sentences carry only two distinct meanings.

**What "except" adds.** "All balls are round except balls used in rugby" does two things. It states a rule for the non-rugby balls (they are round), and it marks the rugby balls as the exception (they are not round). Together that is a biconditional, $R \Leftrightarrow \neg G$: being round and being a rugby ball are mutually exclusive, and together they cover every ball. In disjunction form it is $(G \lor R) \land (\neg G \lor \neg R)$, with one clause per half.

**Quantifiers and conjunction.** $\forall x$ distributes over $\land$, so two universally quantified sentences joined by $\land$ can be checked object by object. That reduces the question to a four-row truth table for a single ball.

**Back to this question.** The assertion needs one sentence from each contrapositive pair: one from $\{s1, s2\}$ for the rule and one from $\{s3, s4\}$ for the exception. $s1 \land s3$ (A) and $s2 \land s3$ (C) do that. $s1 \land s2$ (B) and $s3 \land s4$ (D) repeat one half twice. The answer is **(A), (C)**.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation:
$s1 \equiv  orall \mathit{ball}\,(G \lor R)$ says every non-rugby ball is round, and $s3 \equiv  orall \mathit{ball}\,(
eg G \lor 
eg R)$ says no rugby ball is round. Together they give $R \Leftrightarrow 
eg G$ for every ball, which is exactly the assertion.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $s2$ is the contrapositive of $s1$, so $s1 \land s2 \equiv s1$: it only says that non-rugby balls are round. It allows a round rugby ball ($G = R = \text{T}$), which the exception clause of the assertion excludes.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation:
$s2$ ($
eg R \Rightarrow G$) is equivalent to $s1$, so $s2 \land s3$ is the same formula as (A): $ orall \mathit{ball}\,[(G \lor R) \land (
eg G \lor 
eg R)]$, i.e. round if and only if not used in rugby.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $s4$ is the contrapositive of $s3$, so $s3 \land s4 \equiv s3$: it only says that no rugby ball is round. It allows a ball that is neither used in rugby nor round ($G = R = \text{F}$), which contradicts "all balls are round" for non-rugby balls.

solution.shortcut: Spot the contrapositive pairs: $s1 \equiv s2$ and $s3 \equiv s4$. A correct representation needs both halves (non-rugby $\Rightarrow$ round, and rugby $\Rightarrow$ not round), so it must take one sentence from each pair. (B) and (D) pair a sentence with its own contrapositive and fail; (A) and (C) mix the pairs and work.
solution.commonTrap: Choosing (B) because "all balls are round except rugby balls" is read only as "non-rugby balls are round". $s1$ and $s2$ are contrapositives, not different facts, so (B) is just $s1$ written twice, and it would allow a round rugby ball. The official key (A, C) reads the exception as saying the rugby balls are **not** round, so both halves are needed. A second slip is to treat $s2$ as the converse of $s1$ and conclude that $s1 \land s2$ is the biconditional; the converse of $\neg G \Rightarrow R$ would be $R \Rightarrow \neg G$, which is $s4$, not $s2$.

answerVerification.method: Blind independent re-solve + Python check agrees with official key
answerVerification.notes: Blind re-solve: with G = game(ball, rugby) and R = shape(ball, round), s1 ≡ s2 ≡ ∀ball (G ∨ R) and s3 ≡ s4 ≡ ∀ball (¬G ∨ ¬R) (contrapositive pairs). Reading "all balls are round except balls used in rugby" as round ⟺ not rugby for every ball, the representation needs one sentence from each pair, giving A;C. The stored Python check (brute force over every interpretation of the two predicates on domains of 1 to 3 balls) confirms s1 ≡ s2, s3 ≡ s4, that A and C are equivalent to ∀ball (R ⟺ ¬G), that B is equivalent only to the weaker ∀ball (¬G ⟹ R), and that D matches neither reading. This agrees with the official key A;C. Interpretive note: under the weaker reading (only 'non-rugby balls are round'), B alone would be the exact translation; the official key adopts the standard reading in which the exception clause also asserts that rugby balls are not round.
